analysis.title: Emerging Markets Weekly: Mexico: Things are looking up
key_insights: Mexico's growth has rebounded from a very weak 2025. Q3 GDP grew 0.9% qoq and 3.2% yoy, above expectations, up from 2.1% yoy in Q2 and the highest in 2 years.

AI-related exports to the US are the main driver. Mexico is the only Latin American country that has benefited directly from the AI investment boom, assembling servers that enter the US duty-free under the USMCA with no stringent rules of origin.

Exports of servers and related hardware have grown more than 100% yoy in recent months and now make up 40% of total exports, against about 20% two years ago. Electrical and electronic equipment has overtaken autos as the biggest export category.
Mexico's value-added in these exports is low because most parts, such as semiconductors, come from Asia (Korea, Taiwan, China, ASEAN). The exports still support a trade surplus in 2026.
Auto exports face stricter USMCA rules of origin, with 25% tariffs on non-US content. Vehicle export volumes have fallen recently.

Imports from China are up about 7% on a 12-month rolling basis despite tariffs of up to 50% on Chinese goods since the start of the year. Imports of steel and vehicles fell, while imports of untariffed electrical machinery were robust. China's electronic components reach the US via Mexico.

Investment is recovering, led by construction, as public and private projects take off under President Sheinbaum's Plan Mexico. About half of the Plan's projects are in energy, focused on renewables and grid modernisation. Rail, Mexico City metro and highway projects are under construction, with more starting in 2027 before the June midterm elections.
The capex cycle could sustain and broaden with a US-Mexico trade deal. Consumption growth has been modest.

Banxico is expected to be on hold for some time with inflation within the target band. The latest cut, made despite higher headline inflation, shows a pro-growth committee and could undermine its credibility. Ongoing recovery raises upside inflation risks, and lower rates have already supported credit growth.
A narrower interest rate differential with the US will likely keep the MXN weak, even with a trade surplus and steady remittances.

The 2027 budget projects a fiscal deficit of 3.9% of GDP, against a 4.1% forecast for 2026. With improving growth, this should keep Mexico's lowest investment grade rating from agencies for the next 6-12 months, so no downgrade to high yield.

Stricter USMCA rules of origin and 25% tariffs on non-US content have cut vehicle export volumes.

risk_factors: Low Mexican value-added in AI hardware exports, since most components are imported from Asia.
Stricter USMCA rules of origin and 25% tariffs on non-US content are hurting auto exports.
Ongoing recovery raises upside risks to inflation, and Banxico's surprise cut could undermine its credibility.
A narrower interest rate differential with the US puts downward pressure on the MXN.
geopolitical: USMCA duty-free treatment for Mexican computer hardware exports to the US, with stricter rules of origin and 25% tariffs on non-US content for autos.
Mexico raised tariffs of up to 50% on Chinese goods in autos, textiles, clothing, steel, plastics, footwear, furniture, toys, aluminum and glass at the start of the year.
A possible US-Mexico trade deal could sustain and broaden the capex cycle.
Mexican midterm elections in June 2027, ahead of which more infrastructure projects break ground.
